cards.explanation: The answer is that David says he is poor and needy. He leans in and says, "…for I am poor and needy." No résumé, no list of favors, just "I need help." I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so I know how honest that feels. I think it's a mighty fine way to knock on God's door, friends.
The answer is False. David says, "…for I call to You all day long." That's the opposite of once in a while, friends. All day means all day, and I love it.

The answer is kind and forgiving. David says, "For You, O Lord, are kind and forgiving, rich in loving devotion to all who call on You." Kind and forgiving, that's the word he picks. Look at that last part, bakers: the loving devotion is for all who call on Him. I'd keep calling too.

The answer is answers. David says, "In the day of my distress I call on You, because You answer me." That's his reason. He calls because he knows Someone picks up. Plenty of people call a customer service line with no idea if anyone ever will.

The answer is that the nations will come and bow before Him. David says, "All the nations You have made will come and bow before You, O Lord, and they will glorify Your name." Think about that, friends. One man in one prayer, and he's looking at every nation. He starts small and ends up looking at the whole planet.

The answer is True. David says, "For You are great and perform wonders; You alone are God." He doesn't say God is one of a few, friends. He doesn't say God is the best of the bunch. He says God alone is God.

The answer is way. David prays, "Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth." He wants to be taught and then to walk in it. Learning without walking is like reading the recipe and never turning on the oven. David wants both, bakers.

The answer is so that he may fear God's name. David prays, "Give me an undivided heart, that I may fear Your name." That's what he wants it for, friends. He asks for an undivided heart, and fearing God's name is the reason he gives.

The answer is that God delivered him from the depths of Sheol. David says, "You have delivered me from the depths of Sheol." That's a heavy line, friends. And he says it right after calling God's loving devotion to him great. I think David isn't saying it lightly.

The answer is True, and look where David says it. Right after ruthless men come after him, he says, "But You, O Lord, are a compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness." He looks at the trouble and then at God. I want that kind of focus, bakers.

The answer is enemies. David asks, "Show me a sign of Your goodness, that my enemies may see and be ashamed…" He wants the very people against him to see it. And he says the Lord has helped him and comforted him (Psalm 86:17). He's asking from experience, friends.

The answer is False. David ends with, "for You, O LORD, have helped me and comforted me." He started this prayer poor and needy, and he finishes by saying God helped, friends. I'd close a prayer like that every time.
